name: Double-jaw surgery for retrognathia

card.summary: Bimaxillary (upper and lower jaw) surgery that moves a recessed mandible forward, often with the maxilla and chin; a major established operation with documented joint and nerve risks.
card.aka: Bimaxillary surgery, bimax, BSSO plus Le Fort I, DJS
card.note: Major surgery: reported complications include nerve injury, infection and condylar changes; forum users debate single-jaw versus double-jaw plans.

quick.overview:
Double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery repositions both the upper and lower jaw, usually after orthodontic preparation, to correct a recessed lower jaw (retrognathia), bite problems and facial proportions. It is a long-established operation in oral and maxillofacial surgery, and sometimes is combined with a genioplasty.

In looksmaxxing communities it sits at the top of the 'hardmaxxing' ladder, and members discuss whether a single-jaw plan can do the job.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons cut the jaws (typically a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the mandible and a Le Fort I osteotomy of the maxilla), move them to a planned position, and fix them with plates and screws. Planning uses imaging and often 3D software.
quick.risks: Reported risks include temporary or permanent numbness from nerve injury, infection, bleeding and swelling, and in some patients condylar atrophy or joint changes after bimaxillary surgery. Recovery is typically measured in weeks to months.

lead: Double-jaw surgery, or bimaxillary surgery, is an orthognathic operation in which both the maxilla (upper jaw) and the mandible (lower jaw) are cut, repositioned and fixed. For retrognathia, a recessed lower jaw, the mandible is advanced, commonly through a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, and the upper jaw is moved to match the bite. [1][2]

Orthognathic surgery is described as corrective jaw surgery usually done through the mouth, in coordination with an orthodontist. Encyclopedic accounts trace its development from a case published in 1849 through the mid-twentieth-century popularisation of the sagittal split by Hugo Obwegeser. [1] A 1957 paper on correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia considered genioplasty as part of surgical reshaping of the chin. [3]
In looksmaxxing forums, double-jaw surgery is discussed as a major hardmaxxing option, with threads comparing it with single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty. [4][5]
infobox: Mandibular sagittal split, Le Fort I osteotomy, optional genioplasty
Initial healing about 2 to 6 weeks, bone healing a few further months [2]
Orthodontic camouflage, single-jaw surgery, genioplasty, implants

paras: Orthognathic surgery addresses jaw structure and growth problems, airway issues including sleep apnea, joint disorders, malocclusion and facial asymmetry or proportion. [1] The bilateral sagittal split osteotomy moves the mandible forward or backward. [1]
A 1957 paper reported surgical procedures to correct mandibular prognathism and retrognathia and the reshaping of the chin. [3]
Encyclopedic accounts list bleeding, swelling, infection, and nerve damage causing facial numbness, which is usually temporary but rarely permanent; infection rates of up to 7% are reported. [2]
A 1984 review examined complications after mandibular sagittal split osteotomy, and a 1990 paper reported condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery. [6][7]

A looksmax.org thread discusses single-jaw surgery combined with genioplasty for skeletal class II retrognathia compared with double-jaw surgery, referring to a study comparing conventional bimaxillary surgery with single-jaw surgery using autorotation. [4] A reply states that both jaws usually need to be moved because of the bite plane and tooth alignment unless one jaw is already well positioned. [4]

Published literature includes the 1957 surgical description [3], a 1984 complications review of sagittal split osteotomy [6] and a 1990 study of condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery. [7] Registered trials of retrognathia are mostly of non-surgical orthodontic treatments, such as functional appliances and clear-aligner mandibular advancement. [8][9]

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-surgery cases. [1]
Paper on correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia with genioplasty is published. [3]
Complications after mandibular sagittal split osteotomy are reviewed. [6]
Condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery reported. [7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, double-jaw surgery appears in planning threads and discussions of whether a recessed lower jaw can be treated with one jaw operation plus genioplasty. [4][5]

claims.claim: Single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty can match double-jaw results
claims.believers: A poster planning upper-jaw movement with genioplasty cites a study reporting similar absolute movements between the groups and asks why more single-jaw cases are not seen. [4]
claims.experts: Surgical practice generally plans movements around bite and tooth alignment; a forum reply states that both jaws usually need moving unless one jaw is well positioned. No controlled trial is cited in the sources reviewed. [4]

claims.claim: Retrognathia is a diagnosable skeletal deformity that can be treated surgically
claims.believers: One poster describes seeing a maxillofacial surgeon and hoping the diagnosis supports reconstructive treatment. [5]
claims.experts: Orthognathic surgery is an established specialty for jaw position problems, with documented risks including nerve injury and condylar changes. [2][7]
